events.title: Vellore Mutiny
events.summary: On 10 July 1806 Indian sepoys at Vellore rose against new dress rules and killed many British officers.
events.detail:
The Madras army issued new rules: sepoys had to wear a new round turban, remove caste marks from their foreheads and trim their beards. Hindu and Muslim sepoys both saw this as an attack on their religion.

Tipu Sultan's sons were imprisoned in Vellore fort, and the rebels raised the Mysore flag. Within hours a British cavalry force under Colonel Gillespie rode in from Arcot and crushed the rising.

sides.name: East India Company
sides.ruler: Sir George Barlow, acting Governor-General; Lord William Bentinck, Governor of Madras

sides.name: Sepoys of Vellore
sides.ruler: No single leader; Tipu's sons were their figureheads

causes: New dress code: a new turban, no caste marks, trimmed beards and moustaches.
Sepoys feared it was a step towards making them Christians.

About 100 British soldiers and officers are killed.
The Mysore flag is raised over the fort.
Colonel Gillespie arrives from Arcot within hours and retakes the fort.
losses: British: about 100 killed.
Sepoys: several hundred killed in the fighting or executed afterwards.
outcomes: The new dress rules were withdrawn.
Bentinck and the commander-in-chief were recalled.
Tipu's family was moved to Calcutta.
Seen as a forerunner of 1857: sepoys rising over religion.
facts: Vellore Mutiny: 10 July 1806.
Lord William Bentinck was Governor of Madras then; he became Governor-General later (1828).

pairs.right: New turban and ban on caste marks

participants.role: Governor of Madras; recalled to Britain after the mutiny.

events.after: Sepoys killed about 100 British soldiers; the revolt was crushed in a day; Governor **William Bentinck** was recalled.
events.today: Seen as a forerunner of 1857, 51 years earlier.

events.title: Treaty of Amritsar: the Sutlej becomes a border
events.summary: On 25 April 1809 Ranjit Singh and the Company agreed that the Sutlej would be the boundary between them.
events.detail:
Ranjit Singh had united the Sikh misls and wanted the Sikh states south of the Sutlej too. The Company, worried about a French invasion through the north-west, wanted a friendly Punjab.

Lord Minto sent Charles Metcalfe to Lahore. Ranjit Singh agreed to stay north of the Sutlej; the states south of it (cis-Sutlej) came under British protection.
causes: Fear of a French attack on India through Persia and Afghanistan (Napoleon).
Ranjit Singh's attempts to take the Sikh states south of the Sutlej.

treaties.name: Treaty of Amritsar
terms: The Sutlej river would be the boundary.
The cis-Sutlej Sikh states came under British protection.
Ranjit Singh was free to expand north and west of the Sutlej.
Perpetual friendship between the two.

gains: Company: a safe frontier and a friendly Punjab.
Ranjit Singh: a free hand to conquer Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar.
losses: Ranjit Singh: his claim to the cis-Sutlej states.
outcomes: Peace with the Punjab lasted till Ranjit Singh's death (1839).
facts: Treaty of Amritsar: 1809, between Ranjit Singh and the Company (envoy Charles Metcalfe, under Lord Minto I).
A second Treaty of Amritsar (1846) sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh — do not confuse the two.
Treaty-governor pairs: Salbai 1782 — Warren Hastings; Bassein 1802 — Wellesley; Amritsar 1809 — Minto-I; Lahore 1846 — Hardinge-I (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).
events.yearHook: Two Treaties of Amritsar: 1809 (Sutlej border) and 1846 (Kashmir sold) — 37 years apart.

participants.role: Signed the treaty and gave up his claim to the cis-Sutlej states.
The Company's envoy who negotiated the treaty at Lahore.
Governor-General who sent Metcalfe.

events.after: He agreed to stay north of the **Sutlej** and kept friendship with the British till his death (1839), building the Khalsa army with European officers.
events.today: The Sutlej is still a key boundary river in Punjab.

events.title: Charter Act of 1813
events.summary: Ends the Company's monopoly of Indian trade (except tea and China), sets aside Rs 1 lakh a year for education and lets missionaries in.
events.detail:
British merchants wanted a share of the India trade, and missionaries wanted to work in India. Parliament renewed the Company's charter for 20 years but opened India's trade to all British merchants.

Until 1813 the Company had opposed missionary activities in India (NCERT); the Act allowed them in. It also set aside Rs 1 lakh a year for education — the first time the Company accepted a duty to educate Indians.
causes: British manufacturers and merchants demanded free trade with India.
Missionary groups pressed to be allowed to preach in India.
course: 1813: Parliament renews the charter for 20 years.
Trade with India opened to all British merchants.
The Company keeps only the tea trade and the trade with China.
Rs 1 lakh a year set aside for education.
Missionaries allowed to work in India.
gains: British merchants: free trade with India.
losses: The Company: its trade monopoly in India.
outcomes: Cheap British machine-made goods began to flood India.
The education grant began a debate between Orientalists and Anglicists.
facts: Until 1813, the East India Company was opposed to missionary activities in India (NCERT).
First state money for education: Rs 1 lakh a year.

pairs.right: End of trade monopoly except tea and China

events.yearHook: Charter Acts every 20 years: 1793, 1813, 1833, 1853.

participants.role: Governor-General when the Act was passed.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 6; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: Free-trade ideas (Adam Smith) and British manufacturers attacked the Company's monopoly.
events.after: Indian trade was opened to all British merchants (except tea and China); Rs 1 lakh a year was set aside for education; missionaries were allowed in.
events.today: The Rs 1 lakh grant is called the first state step towards education in India.

events.title: Anglo-Nepal War and the Treaty of Sugauli
events.summary: The Company fights the Gorkha kingdom of Nepal (1814–16); Nepal gives up Kumaon, Garhwal and the Terai.
events.detail:
The Gorkhas of Nepal had expanded along the Himalaya from Sikkim to the Sutlej and clashed with the Company over the Terai border. Lord Hastings declared war in 1814.

The Gorkhas fought hard, but David Ochterlony defeated Amar Singh Thapa at Malaun (1815). Nepal signed the Treaty of Sugauli and ratified it in March 1816.
events.place: The Himalayan foothills from Kumaon to the Terai

sides.name: Nepal
sides.ruler: King Girvan Yuddha Bikram Shah (Prime Minister Bhimsen Thapa)

causes: Border disputes in the Terai between Nepal and Company territory.
Gorkha expansion along the whole Himalayan foothills.
course: 1814: Company armies invade on several fronts; early defeats.
1815: Ochterlony defeats Amar Singh Thapa at Malaun.
December 1815: Treaty of Sugauli signed.
March 1816: Ochterlony advances towards Kathmandu; Nepal ratifies the treaty.

treaties.name: Treaty of Sugauli
terms: Nepal gave up Kumaon and Garhwal.
It gave up much of the Terai and its claims over Sikkim.
A British Resident was placed at Kathmandu.

The British began recruiting Gorkha soldiers.
losses: Nepal: about a third of its territory.
outcomes: Nepal stayed independent but friendly to the British.
facts: Treaty of Sugauli (1816) ended the Anglo-Nepal War under Lord Hastings.

alsoOn.text: Ochterlony defeats Amar Singh Thapa at Malaun; the Treaty of Sugauli is signed (December).
Nepal ratifies the Treaty of Sugauli.

participants.role: Governor-General who declared war.

events.after: By the **Treaty of Sugauli** (1816) Nepal lost Kumaon, Garhwal and Sikkim claims, and accepted a British Resident; the British began recruiting **Gurkha** soldiers.
events.today: Gurkha regiments serve in the Indian and British armies; Shimla, Mussoorie and Nainital grew in the lands gained.

events.title: Paika uprising at Khurda
events.summary: On 29 March 1817 the Paiks of Khurda (Orissa) rose under Buxi Jagabandhu against British rule (NCERT).
events.detail:
The British took Orissa in 1803 and annexed Khurda after deposing its Raja, Mukunda Dev II. They took away the service lands of the Paiks — Khurda's old militia — raised the revenue again and again, and sold the lands of defaulters (NCERT).

Buxi Jagabandhu, Khurda's hereditary military commander, had lost his estate and lived on gifts from the people. He led the Paiks in an armed uprising. It was the first popular armed rising against the British in Orissa (NCERT).

sides.name: Paiks of Khurda
sides.ruler: Raja Mukunda Dev II (declared by the rebels)

causes: The British took away the Paiks' service lands (NCERT).
Revenue demands rose again and again, with no relief in bad years (NCERT).
Revenue had to be paid in the new silver sicca rupee (NCERT).
The salt monopoly ruined Orissa's salt makers and raised prices (NCERT).
Estates were auctioned in Calcutta to absentee landlords from Bengal (NCERT).
A corrupt and harsh police (NCERT).
course: 29 March 1817: Paiks attack the police station at Banpur, kill over a hundred men and take government money (NCERT).
A no-rent campaign begins; zamindars and ryots join (NCERT).
14 April 1817: Buxi Jagabandhu, with 5,000–10,000 Paiks and Kandhs, seizes Puri and declares Mukunda Dev II ruler (NCERT).
The British declare martial law, capture the Raja and send Major-General Martindell (NCERT).
By May 1817 the rising is mostly put down; Buxi Jagabandhu fights on until he surrenders in May 1825 (NCERT).
losses: Hundreds of Paiks were killed; many fled to the jungles (NCERT).
outcomes: The British adopted a policy of "leniency, indulgence and forbearance" towards Khurda (NCERT).
The salt price was cut, corrupt officials were dismissed and old landholders got their lands back (NCERT).
It was the first popular anti-British armed uprising in Orissa (NCERT).
facts: The Paika uprising began on 29 March 1817 (NCERT).
Its leader was Buxi Jagabandhu, hereditary military commander of the Raja of Khurda (NCERT).
Puri was seized on 14 April 1817 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Buxi Jagabandhu, leader of the Paika uprising, surrenders (NCERT).

events.yearHook: Forty years before 1857: 1857 − 40 = 1817.

participants.role: Led the uprising, seized Puri and kept fighting until 1825.
Deposed Raja whom the Paiks declared their ruler; captured and jailed at Cuttack.
Governor-General at the time.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 5 "When People Revolt" (The Khurda Uprising – A Case Study)
events.before: The British took Odisha (1803); the **Paikas** (militia of the Khurda raja) lost their rent-free lands; salt and cowrie money changes hurt the people.
events.after: **Bakshi Jagabandhu** led the Paikas; the rising was crushed by 1818–19.
events.today: Odisha calls it the "First War of Independence"; its bicentenary was marked in 2017.

events.title: Pindari War
events.summary: Lord Hastings hunts down the Pindaris, bands of raiders who plundered central India.
events.detail:
The Pindaris were irregular horsemen who had served the Maratha armies and lived by plunder. With Maratha power declining, they raided far and wide, even into Company territory.

In 1817 Lord Hastings gathered a huge army to surround and destroy them. Their leaders Chitu, Karim Khan and Wasil Muhammad were scattered; Karim Khan was given land at Gorakhpur.

sides.name: Pindaris
sides.ruler: Leaders Chitu, Karim Khan and Wasil Muhammad

causes: Pindari raids into central India and Company lands.
The Company suspected Maratha chiefs of protecting them.
outcomes: The Pindaris were broken up by 1818.
The campaign merged into the Third Anglo-Maratha War.
events.yearHook: Same year as the Paika uprising — 1817 — the year the last Maratha war began.

participants.role: Organised the campaign against the Pindaris.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
facts: The Lottery Committee (1817, Calcutta, under Lord Hastings) raised money by lotteries for town planning and improvement of Calcutta — roads, drains and tanks (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

events.after: **Hastings** (Lord Moira) crushed them; leaders like **Chitu** were killed and **Amir Khan** became Nawab of **Tonk**.
events.today: Tonk (Rajasthan) was a princely state until 1948.

events.title: Third Anglo-Maratha War: the Peshwa falls
events.summary: The Company defeats the Peshwa, Bhonsle and Holkar (1817–19); the Peshwa is removed and sent to Bithur (NCERT).
events.detail:
In June 1817 the British forced Baji Rao II to sign the Treaty of Poona, giving up his headship of the Maratha confederacy. Angry, he attacked the British Residency at Poona in November 1817. Bhonsle of Nagpur and the Holkar army also rose.

The Marathas were beaten at Khadki, Sitabuldi, Mahidpur, Koregaon and Ashti. Baji Rao surrendered in 1818. The Peshwa was removed and sent away to Bithur near Kanpur with a pension. The Company now had complete control over the territories south of the Vindhyas (NCERT).
events.place: Poona, Nagpur, Malwa and the Deccan

sides.name: Marathas
sides.ruler: Peshwa Baji Rao II, with Appa Sahib Bhonsle (Nagpur) and the Holkar army

causes: Lord Hastings's policy of paramountcy: the Company claimed its authority was supreme over Indian states (NCERT).
Treaty of Poona (June 1817): the Peshwa was made to give up his headship of the Maratha confederacy.
The Pindari campaign brought British armies into Maratha territory.
course: November 1817: the Peshwa attacks the Poona Residency; beaten at Khadki.
November 1817: Appa Sahib Bhonsle beaten at Sitabuldi (Nagpur).
December 1817: the Holkar army beaten at Mahidpur.
1 January 1818: Battle of Koregaon.
February 1818: Peshwa beaten at Ashti.
June 1818: Baji Rao II surrenders.

treaties.name: Treaty of Poona
terms: The Peshwa gave up his headship of the Maratha confederacy.
He ceded more territory.

treaties.name: Treaty of Mandsaur
terms: Holkar accepted a subsidiary alliance and gave up lands.

losses: Marathas: the office of Peshwa abolished; their lands annexed (NCERT).
gains: Company: complete control south of the Vindhyas (NCERT); the Bombay Presidency greatly enlarged.
outcomes: The Peshwa was removed and sent to Bithur near Kanpur with a pension (NCERT).
A small state of Satara was created for Shivaji's descendant Pratap Singh.
Maratha power came to an end (NCERT).
facts: The Third Anglo-Maratha War was fought in 1817–19 (NCERT).
After it the Peshwa was sent to Bithur near Kanpur with a pension (NCERT).
Lord Hastings (1813–23) started the policy of paramountcy (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Baji Rao II surrenders; the office of Peshwa is abolished. First revenue settlement in the Bombay Deccan (NCERT).

participants.role: Last Peshwa; attacked the Residency, lost, surrendered and was pensioned off to Bithur.
Resident at Poona; won at Khadki and then ruled the Peshwa's lands.
Governor-General; started the policy of paramountcy (NCERT).
Founder of the Maratha state whose line ruled Satara.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)

images.alt: Third Anglo-Maratha War: the Peshwa falls

events.before: The Peshwa chafed under British control; the Pindari war gave a reason.
events.after: The Peshwa was beaten at **Koregaon** (1818) and **Kirkee**; the Peshwa-ship was abolished, **Baji Rao II** pensioned off at **Bithur** (his adopted son was **Nana Saheb**, of 1857).
events.today: Bhima-Koregaon (1 January 1818) is remembered by Dalits as a victory of Mahar soldiers.
events.mnemonic: Maratha wars end-treaties "S-B-P": Salbai (1782), Bassein (1802), Poona (1817).

events.title: Ryotwari settlement spreads in Madras
events.summary: Thomas Munro, now Governor of Madras, extends the ryotwari system across south India (NCERT).
events.detail:
In the south there were no traditional zamindars, argued Alexander Read and Thomas Munro. So the revenue settlement had to be made directly with the cultivators (ryots) who had tilled the land for generations (NCERT).

Each field was surveyed separately before the revenue was fixed. Munro believed the British should act as parental fathers protecting the ryots. But the revenue fixed was so high that peasants fled the countryside (NCERT).
causes: The Permanent Settlement had fixed revenue for ever; the Company needed more money (NCERT).
There were no traditional zamindars in the south (NCERT).
course: Captain Alexander Read tries it in lands taken from Tipu (NCERT).
Munro develops it in the Ceded Districts (1800–07).
1820: Munro becomes Governor of Madras and extends it all over south India (NCERT).
gains: Company: higher revenue that could be revised.
losses: Ryots: the revenue was too high; many fled (NCERT).
outcomes: Ryotwari covered Madras and, later, the Bombay Presidency.
facts: Ryotwari was tried by Alexander Read and developed by Thomas Munro (NCERT).
Revenue was settled directly with the ryots, not zamindars (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1793 Permanent → 1820 Ryotwari → 1822 Mahalwari: zamindar, then ryot, then village.

participants.role: Developed the system and, as Governor of Madras, extended it over south India.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 3 "Ruling the Countryside"
events.before: **Alexander Read** and **Thomas Munro** had tried the ryotwari system in the **Baramahal** and the **Ceded Districts** (Rayalaseema).
events.after: Each peasant (ryot) dealt directly with the state; revenue was high (often half the produce) and fixed for 30 years. Debt and land sales to moneylenders followed, leading to the **Deccan riots** (1875).
events.today: Andhra's patta and the village revenue officer (VRO) system descend from ryotwari.

events.title: Mahalwari settlement (Holt Mackenzie)
events.summary: In the North-Western Provinces, revenue is settled village by village and collected by the headman (NCERT).
events.detail:
Holt Mackenzie felt that the village was an important social institution in north India and should be kept (NCERT). Collectors went from village to village, measured the fields and recorded the rights of different groups.

The revenue of all the plots in a village (mahal) was added up. The village headman, not a zamindar, collected it, and the demand was revised from time to time, not fixed for ever (NCERT).
events.place: North-Western Provinces of the Bengal Presidency (now mostly Uttar Pradesh)
causes: The Company needed more revenue than the Permanent Settlement allowed (NCERT).
course: Collectors survey every village, measure fields and record customs and rights (NCERT).
Revenue is fixed for the whole village (mahal) (NCERT).
The village headman collects and pays it (NCERT).
outcomes: Revenue demand was periodically revised, not permanent (NCERT).
Later extended to Punjab and parts of central India.
facts: Mahalwari was devised by Holt Mackenzie and came into effect in 1822 (NCERT).
Mahal = estate or village in British revenue records (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Two years after Munro's ryotwari (1820) — 1822.

participants.role: Devised the mahalwari system (NCERT).

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 3
events.before: In the North-Western Provinces and Punjab, land was often held jointly by village communities.
events.after: Revenue was fixed for the village (**mahal**) as a whole and collected by the headman; **Bentinck** and **R. M. Bird** revised it (1833).
events.today: About 30% of British India was under mahalwari.

events.title: Rani Channamma of Kittur rises against the British
events.summary: When the British tried to annex Kittur, its queen Rani Channamma took up arms (NCERT).
events.detail:
Kittur was a small state in today's Karnataka. Its ruler died without a natural heir, and the British refused to accept Rani Channamma's adopted son. When they tried to take over the state, she led an armed resistance (NCERT).

She was arrested in 1824 and died in prison in 1829. Rayanna, a poor chowkidar of Sangoli, carried on the struggle until he was caught and hanged (NCERT).
causes: The British refused to recognise the Rani's adopted son as heir.
The policy of paramountcy: the Company felt free to annex any state (NCERT).
course: October 1824: the British besiege Kittur; their political agent Thackeray is killed.
A larger force takes the fort; the Rani is arrested in 1824 (NCERT).
Rayanna carries on guerrilla resistance, destroying British camps and records (NCERT).
losses: Kittur: annexed; the Rani died in prison (1829) (NCERT).
outcomes: Rani Channamma became a symbol of resistance in Karnataka.
facts: Rani Channamma was arrested in 1824 and died in prison in 1829 (NCERT).
Rayanna of Sangoli carried on the resistance; NCERT says he was hanged in 1830.

alsoOn.text: Rani Channamma of Kittur dies in prison (NCERT).
Rayanna of Sangoli is caught and hanged by the British (NCERT).

events.yearHook: Same year as the Barrackpore mutiny and the first Burmese war — 1824.

participants.role: Queen who led the armed resistance; arrested in 1824.
Carried on the resistance with popular support; hanged.
Governor-General at the time.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2
events.before: The Company refused to accept the adopted son of Kittur's late chief — an early case of the lapse idea.
events.after: Rani **Chennamma** beat a British force (Thackeray killed, October 1824) but was captured and died in prison (1829); **Sangolli Rayanna** fought on till 1831.
events.today: Kittur Utsav is held each October in Karnataka; her statue stands in the Parliament complex.

events.title: First Anglo-Burmese War and the Treaty of Yandabo
events.summary: The Company fights Burma (1824–26); by the Treaty of Yandabo Burma gives up Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim.
events.detail:
Burma had conquered Assam and Manipur and threatened Bengal's border. Lord Amherst declared war in 1824. Disease killed far more British soldiers than the fighting.

After the Burmese general Maha Bandula was killed (1825), the British advanced up the Irrawaddy. Burma signed the Treaty of Yandabo in February 1826.
causes: Burmese conquest of Assam and Manipur.
Border clashes on the Bengal frontier (Chittagong).

treaties.name: Treaty of Yandabo
terms: Burma gave up Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim.
It paid a war indemnity of 1 crore rupees.
A British Resident was accepted at Ava.

gains: Company: Assam and the north-east; Arakan and Tenasserim.
losses: Burma: large territories and money.
Company: about 15,000 soldiers, mostly to disease.
facts: Treaty of Yandabo (1826) ended the First Anglo-Burmese War under Lord Amherst; Assam came under British control.

alsoOn.text: Treaty of Yandabo: Burma cedes Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim.

events.yearHook: Burmese wars: 1824, 1852, 1885 — one under Amherst, Dalhousie and Dufferin.

participants.role: Governor-General who declared war and made the peace.
Burmese commander; killed in 1825.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)

images.alt: First Anglo-Burmese War and the Treaty of Yandabo

outcomes: Assam and the north-east came under British control.
Burma lost its coastal provinces; war resumed in 1852.
events.before: Burma had taken **Assam**, Manipur and Arakan and threatened Bengal.
events.after: By the **Treaty of Yandabo** (1826) Burma gave up Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim; the British began **tea** in Assam.

events.title: Barrackpore sepoys refuse to sail to Burma
events.summary: Sepoys at Barrackpore refuse to go to Burma by sea, because crossing the sea would cost them their caste (NCERT).
events.detail:
Many people then believed that crossing the sea meant losing one's religion and caste. In 1824 sepoys at Barrackpore were ordered to go to Burma by sea. They refused, though they agreed to go by land (NCERT).

They were severely punished. The issue did not die down; in 1856 the Company passed a law that every new recruit had to agree to serve overseas (NCERT).
causes: Fear of losing caste by crossing the sea (NCERT).
Lack of transport and allowances for the march.
losses: Many sepoys were killed or severely punished (NCERT).
outcomes: The General Service Enlistment Act (1856) made every new recruit agree to serve overseas (NCERT) — a cause of 1857.
facts: In 1824 the sepoys at Barrackpore refused to go to Burma by sea (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Barrackpore again in 1857: Mangal Pandey — two sepoy protests at the same place.

participants.role: Governor-General at the time.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 5
events.before: High-caste sepoys believed crossing the sea broke caste rules; they were ordered to Burma.
events.after: The 47th Native Infantry refused and was fired on; the same fear returned in **1856** (General Service Enlistment Act).
events.today: Barrackpore saw the first shot of 1857 too (Mangal Pandey, March 1857).

events.title: Suppression of Thuggee
events.summary: Bentinck and William Sleeman break up the Thugs, gangs who strangled and robbed travellers.
events.detail: Thugs were organised gangs who joined travellers on the roads, strangled them and robbed them. Under Bentinck, William Sleeman used informers (approvers) to track the gangs down. By the late 1830s thousands had been arrested.
outcomes: Thuggee was practically wiped out by about 1840.
events.yearHook: Bentinck's reforms: sati 1829, Thuggee from 1830, English education 1835.

participants.role: Governor-General who ordered the campaign.
Led the campaign.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
causes: Travellers on India's roads were robbed and murdered by organised gangs.
Bentinck wanted to show that British rule brought safety and order.
events.before: Bands of **thugs** murdered travellers on the roads of central India.
events.after: Captain **William Sleeman** broke the gangs (1830s); thuggee was nearly gone by 1840.
events.today: Sleemanabad (MP) is named after him; "thug" entered English.

events.title: Kol uprising
events.summary: The Kols of Chotanagpur rise (1831–32) against outsiders who took their lands (NCERT).
events.detail: Tribal groups rebelled against new laws, taxes and exploitation by traders and moneylenders (NCERT). In Chotanagpur, land was handed over to outsiders (dikus) — moneylenders, traders and Sikh and Muslim farmers. The Kols, led by Buddhu Bhagat, rose in 1831–32 and attacked the outsiders. The rising was put down by force.
causes: Tribal lands given to outsiders (dikus).
New taxes and exploitation by moneylenders (NCERT).
outcomes: Crushed by troops; Chotanagpur was later placed under a special administration (South-West Frontier Agency, 1834).
facts: The Kols rebelled in 1831–32 (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Tribal risings in NCERT: Kols 1831, Santhals 1855, Birsa 1899, Bastar 1910, Warli 1940.

participants.role: Governor-General when the rising was suppressed.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 4 "Tribals, Dikus and the Vision of a Golden Age"
events.before: Outsiders (dikus) took Kol (Munda, Ho, Oraon) land in Chotanagpur under British courts.
events.after: The rising was crushed (1832); the area was put under special rule (South-West Frontier Agency).
events.today: Chotanagpur tenancy laws (1908) grew out of these tribal risings.

events.title: The Company takes over Mysore's administration
events.summary: Bentinck takes over the government of Mysore, citing misrule.
events.detail: After a peasant revolt (the Nagar rising) in Mysore, Bentinck accused Krishnaraja Wodeyar III of misrule and placed the state under British commissioners. In 1834 he also annexed Coorg.
outcomes: Mysore stayed under British commissioners until 1881.
events.yearHook: Bentinck annexes Mysore (1831) and Coorg (1834).

participants.role: Took over Mysore and annexed Coorg.
Maharaja removed from power.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
causes: A peasant rising (the Nagar revolt, 1830–31) against heavy taxes.
Bentinck blamed the Maharaja's misrule.
events.before: Peasant revolts (Nagar) broke out against heavy taxes under Krishnaraja Wodeyar III.
events.after: **Bentinck** took over the administration on grounds of misrule; it was given back in 1881 (the "rendition").
events.today: Mysore became one of the most advanced princely states (Visvesvaraya, KRS dam, 1910s–30s).

events.title: Charter Act of 1833
events.summary: Makes the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India and ends the Company's trading role.
events.detail:
Parliament renewed the charter for 20 years but changed the Company's nature: it stopped being a trader and became only a government for India.

The Governor-General of Bengal became the Governor-General of India, with power to make laws for the whole of British India. A Law Member was added to his council, and a Law Commission was set up.
causes: Free-trade pressure in Britain.
The need for one law-making authority for British India.
course: Governor-General of Bengal → Governor-General of India.
The Company's trade — including tea and China — ended.
A fourth (Law) member added to the council.
Section 87: no Indian could be barred from any office because of religion, birth or colour.
A Law Commission was set up to codify Indian laws.
gains: Centralised law-making under the Governor-General of India.
losses: The Company: its trading business.
outcomes: The First Law Commission under Macaulay drafted the Indian Penal Code.
facts: Charter Act 1833 made Lord William Bentinck the first Governor-General of India.
It ended the Company's commercial activities.
events.yearHook: Charter Acts every 20 years: 1793, 1813, 1833, 1853.

participants.role: Became the first Governor-General of India.
First Law Member under the Act (from 1834).

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: The **Charter Act of 1813** had ended the Company's monopoly of Indian trade, except tea and China.
events.after: The Company became a purely administrative body; **Macaulay** joined as the first **Law Member**; the first **Law Commission** prepared the Indian Penal Code (enacted 1860).
events.today: The IPC of 1860 was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 2024.
events.mnemonic: Charter Acts "13-33-53": 1813 (trade monopoly ends except tea and China; Rs 1 lakh for education), 1833 (GG of India; trade ends; Law Member), 1853 (open civil service exam).

events.title: Macaulay's Minute and the English Education Act
events.summary: English becomes the medium of higher education; support for Oriental institutions is cut (NCERT).
events.detail:
Orientalists wanted to promote Indian learning; Anglicists such as Macaulay wanted Western knowledge taught in English. Macaulay's Minute of 2 February 1835 argued that English would make Indians aware of Western science and philosophy (NCERT).

Following the minute, the English Education Act of 1835 was introduced. English became the medium of instruction for higher education, and the promotion of Oriental institutions like the Calcutta Madrasa and Benaras Sanskrit College was stopped (NCERT).
causes: The Rs 1 lakh education grant (1813) started a debate on what to teach.
Anglicists argued that Western learning in English was more useful (NCERT).
course: 2 February 1835: Macaulay's Minute on Indian Education (NCERT).
March 1835: Bentinck's government passes the English Education Act (NCERT).
English textbooks begin to be produced for schools (NCERT).
gains: English-educated Indians: new jobs in government and trade.
losses: Oriental learning: lost state support (NCERT).
outcomes: Created a class of English-educated Indians — later leaders of reform and nationalism.
facts: Macaulay's Minute: 2 February 1835 (NCERT).
The English Education Act of 1835 followed it (NCERT).
Calcutta Medical College was founded the same year (1835).
Metcalfe's Press Act (1835) freed the press.
Charles Metcalfe, acting Governor-General, frees the press (Press Act, 1835).

The Downward Filtration Theory (education) held that English education given to a few upper- and middle-class Indians would filter down to the masses; it was adopted under Macaulay and Auckland and abandoned by Wood's Despatch (1854), which urged vernacular mass education (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

Macaulay's Minute (1835) said that "a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia"; the Orientalists (William Jones, H. T. Colebrooke, H. H. Wilson) defended classical learning (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).
events.yearHook: 1835 = Macaulay's Minute + English Education Act + Metcalfe's Press Act.

participants.role: Wrote the Minute of 2 February 1835.
Governor-General who accepted it.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 6 "Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation"
events.before: The **Orientalists** (Jones, Asiatic Society 1784; Calcutta Madrasa 1781; Sanskrit College Benares 1791) wanted Indian learning; the **Anglicists** wanted English.
events.after: English became the language of higher education and, from 1837, of courts (in place of Persian). **Wood's Despatch** (1854) followed with a full system.
events.today: The "Macaulay's children" debate on English education is still alive.

events.title: Tripartite Treaty
events.summary: Lord Auckland, Ranjit Singh and Shah Shuja agree to put Shah Shuja back on the Afghan throne.
events.detail: In the late 1830s the Company feared that Russia might expand across Asia and enter India from the north-west (NCERT). Auckland decided to replace the Afghan ruler Dost Mohammad, thought to be friendly to Russia, with the ex-king Shah Shuja.
causes: Fear of Russia advancing towards India (NCERT).
Dost Mohammad was seen as unfriendly.

treaties.name: Tripartite Treaty
terms: Shah Shuja would be restored at Kabul with British and Sikh help.
Shah Shuja accepted Ranjit Singh's hold on Peshawar and other Afghan lands.

outcomes: Led straight to the First Anglo-Afghan War (1839–42).
events.yearHook: 1838: the year before the war (1839) and the year before Ranjit Singh died (1839).

participants.role: Governor-General who planned the treaty and the war.
Joined the treaty but sent few troops.
Promised the throne of Kabul.
The Afghan ruler the treaty aimed to remove.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: Britain feared Russia ("the Great Game") and wanted a friendly ruler in Kabul.
events.after: Britain, **Ranjit Singh** and **Shah Shuja** agreed to put Shah Shuja on the Kabul throne, leading to the First Afghan War (1839).
events.today: The "Great Game" phrase is used again for big-power rivalry in Central Asia.

events.title: First Anglo-Afghan War
events.summary: The British invade Afghanistan (1839–42), install Shah Shuja, and suffer a disastrous retreat from Kabul.
events.detail:
Driven by the fear of Russia, the British fought a prolonged war with Afghanistan and established indirect rule there for a while (NCERT). They took Kandahar and Kabul in 1839 and put Shah Shuja on the throne.

In November 1841 Kabul rose in revolt. The British envoy Macnaghten was killed, and in January 1842 the British army retreating to Jalalabad was wiped out in the passes. An "Army of Retribution" retook Kabul in 1842, then withdrew; Dost Mohammad returned.
events.place: Kandahar, Ghazni, Kabul and the Khyber passes

sides.name: Afghans
sides.ruler: Dost Mohammad Khan; later his son Akbar Khan led the revolt

causes: Fear of Russia entering India from the north-west (NCERT).
The Tripartite Treaty (1838).
course: 1839: the British take Kandahar, Ghazni and Kabul; Shah Shuja is crowned.
November 1841: revolt in Kabul; envoy Macnaghten is killed (December).
January 1842: about 16,000 soldiers and camp followers retreat from Kabul; almost all are killed.
September 1842: an army under Pollock retakes Kabul, then withdraws.
losses: British: one of their worst defeats — an entire army destroyed in the retreat.
Huge cost to Indian revenue.
outcomes: Dost Mohammad returned as Amir (1842).
British prestige fell sharply; it influenced the sepoys of 1857.
facts: The Company fought a prolonged war with Afghanistan between 1838 and 1842 (NCERT).
Started by Lord Auckland; ended by Lord Ellenborough.
events.yearHook: Afghan wars: 1839, 1878, 1919 — Auckland, Lytton, Chelmsford.

participants.role: Governor-General who started the war.
Governor-General who ended it and withdrew (1842).
Puppet king at Kabul; killed in 1842.
Deposed in 1839, restored after the war.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: **Dost Mohammad** ruled Kabul; Auckland chose to replace him.
events.after: The British took Kabul, but the revolt of 1841–42 destroyed the retreating army; only Dr **Brydon** reached Jalalabad. Dost Mohammad came back.
events.today: Called "Auckland's folly"; a warning against invading Afghanistan.

events.title: Death of Ranjit Singh; turmoil in the Punjab
events.summary: Ranjit Singh dies in June 1839; within four years three rulers are killed and the boy Duleep Singh becomes Maharaja.
events.detail: The presence of Maharaja Ranjit Singh had held back the Company (NCERT). After his death the court at Lahore fell into factions. Kharak Singh, Nau Nihal Singh and Sher Singh followed one another; Sher Singh was assassinated in 1843 and the five-year-old Duleep Singh became Maharaja under his mother Rani Jindan. Real power passed to the Khalsa army.
outcomes: After his death in 1839, two prolonged wars were fought with the Sikh kingdom (NCERT).
facts: Ranjit Singh died in 1839 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Sher Singh is assassinated; five-year-old Duleep Singh becomes Maharaja of the Punjab.

events.yearHook: Ranjit Singh: Lahore 1799, Amritsar 1809, death 1839 — the "9" years.

participants.role: His death removed the one ruler the British would not attack.
Became Maharaja as a child (1843).
Ruled as regent for her son.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
causes: Ranjit Singh had held the Sikh state together by his own authority.
He left no strong heir; the nobles and the army fought for power.
events.before: Ranjit Singh had built a strong Sikh empire from Lahore to Peshawar and Kashmir.
events.after: Weak heirs and army factions followed; the **First Anglo-Sikh War** came in 1845.
events.today: His **samadhi** is in Lahore; he gave the Golden Temple its gold covering.

events.title: Annexation of Sindh
events.summary: Charles Napier defeats the Amirs of Sindh and the Company annexes Sindh (NCERT).
events.detail:
Sindh, ruled by the Talpur Amirs, lay on the route to Afghanistan. During the Afghan war the British forced treaties on the Amirs; after it, Lord Ellenborough sent Charles Napier to demand more.

Napier defeated the Amirs at Miani (February 1843) and Dubba (March 1843). Sind was taken over in 1843 (NCERT).

sides.name: Amirs of Sindh
sides.ruler: The Talpur Amirs of Hyderabad, Khairpur and Mirpur

causes: Sindh controlled the Indus route to Afghanistan.
The British wanted to make up for the Afghan disaster.
course: February 1843: Napier wins the Battle of Miani.
March 1843: he wins at Dubba near Hyderabad.
1843: Sindh is annexed (NCERT).
losses: Amirs of Sindh: their kingdom.
facts: Sind was taken over in 1843 (NCERT).
Conquered by Charles Napier under Lord Ellenborough.
Slavery is abolished in British India by Act V of 1843 (Lord Ellenborough).
events.yearHook: Afghan war ends 1842 → Sindh taken 1843 → Punjab 1849.

participants.role: Defeated the Amirs and became Governor of Sindh.
Governor-General who approved the annexation.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
outcomes: Sindh was joined to the Bombay Presidency.
The annexation was widely criticised even in Britain.
events.before: The **Amirs of Sindh** had been forced into treaties during the Afghan war.
events.after: **Charles Napier** beat them at **Miani** and annexed Sindh; legend says he signalled "Peccavi" (I have sinned).
events.today: Sindh is a province of Pakistan; Napier's statue is in London's Trafalgar Square.

events.title: First Anglo-Sikh War
events.summary: The Khalsa army crosses the Sutlej (1845); after four battles the Sikhs are beaten and sign the Treaty of Lahore (1846).
events.detail:
After Ranjit Singh's death the Khalsa army was the real power in Lahore. In December 1845 it crossed the Sutlej. The battles of Mudki and Ferozeshah (1845), Aliwal and Sobraon (1846) were hard fought; the Sikh commanders Lal Singh and Tej Singh were suspected of betraying their own army.

The Treaty of Lahore (March 1846) took land and money from the Punjab, and the Treaty of Amritsar sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh.

sides.name: Sikhs (Lahore)
sides.ruler: Maharaja Duleep Singh, with Rani Jindan as regent

causes: Disorder in Lahore after Ranjit Singh's death (NCERT).
British troops massed on the Sutlej border.
The Khalsa army crossed the Sutlej (December 1845).
course: December 1845: battles of Mudki and Ferozeshah.
January 1846: Battle of Aliwal.
February 1846: Battle of Sobraon — the Sikhs are routed.
March 1846: Treaties of Lahore and Amritsar.

treaties.name: Treaty of Lahore
terms: The Jalandhar Doab was ceded.
An indemnity of Rs 1.5 crore was demanded.
The Sikh army was cut down.
A British Resident (Henry Lawrence) at Lahore.

treaties.name: Treaty of Amritsar
terms: Kashmir was sold to Gulab Singh for Rs 75 lakh.

treaties.name: Treaty of Bhairowal
terms: A council of regency under the British Resident would rule until Duleep Singh came of age.
Rani Jindan was removed.

gains: Company: the Jalandhar Doab and control of Lahore.
losses: Punjab: territory, money and real independence.
outcomes: The Punjab became a British-controlled state — the next step was annexation (1849).

alsoOn.text: Treaties of Lahore, Amritsar (Kashmir to Gulab Singh) and Bhairowal end the First Anglo-Sikh War.

events.yearHook: Sikh wars: 1845–46 (Hardinge) and 1848–49 (Dalhousie).

participants.role: Governor-General who fought the war and signed the treaties.
Boy Maharaja; kept his throne under British control.
Regent; removed by the Treaty of Bhairowal.
Stayed neutral and bought Kashmir.
His death (1839) left the Khalsa army as the real power in Lahore.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
events.before: After Ranjit Singh's death the Khalsa army controlled the court; it crossed the Sutlej.
events.after: Battles at **Mudki, Ferozeshah, Aliwal, Sobraon**; by the **Treaty of Lahore** (1846) the Sikhs lost the Jalandhar Doab; **Kashmir** was sold to **Gulab Singh** (Treaty of Amritsar, 1846).
events.today: The 1846 sale of Kashmir is the origin of the Dogra state of Jammu and Kashmir.

events.title: Second Anglo-Sikh War; the Punjab annexed
events.summary: A revolt at Multan grows into a second Sikh war; after Gujrat (1849) the Punjab is annexed (NCERT).
events.detail:
In April 1848 the governor of Multan, Mulraj, revolted and two British officers were killed. Sikh soldiers joined him across the Punjab.

The British fought a bloody, drawn battle at Chillianwala (January 1849) and a decisive one at Gujrat (February 1849). In 1849 Punjab was annexed (NCERT). Duleep Singh was pensioned off and the Koh-i-noor was sent to Queen Victoria.

sides.name: Sikhs
sides.ruler: Rebel governor Mulraj and the Sikh army (Chattar Singh, Sher Singh Attariwala)

causes: Resentment against British control after 1846.
The revolt of Mulraj at Multan (April 1848).
course: April 1848: Mulraj revolts at Multan.
January 1849: Battle of Chillianwala — heavy British losses.
February 1849: Battle of Gujrat — the Sikhs are defeated.
29 March 1849: the Punjab is annexed.
gains: Company: the whole Punjab up to the Afghan frontier.
losses: Sikhs: their kingdom; Duleep Singh deposed; the Koh-i-noor taken.
outcomes: Ultimately, in 1849, Punjab was annexed (NCERT).
The Punjab was run by a Board of Administration (Henry and John Lawrence).
facts: Punjab was annexed in 1849 under Lord Dalhousie (NCERT).
Battle of Gujrat (1849) is called the "battle of the guns".
events.yearHook: Ranjit died 1839; ten years later (1849) his kingdom was gone.

participants.role: Governor-General who fought the war and annexed the Punjab.
Deposed and pensioned.
The Koh-i-noor was sent to her after the annexation.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)

images.alt: Second Anglo-Sikh War; the Punjab annexed
images.credit: J. Harris after H. Martens / Wikimedia Commons

events.before: Revolt at **Multan** (Mulraj) and anger at British control.
events.after: **Chillianwala** and **Gujrat** (1849); Dalhousie annexed the **Punjab** (1849); the young Maharaja **Duleep Singh** was sent to England and the **Koh-i-noor** given to Queen Victoria.
events.today: The Koh-i-noor is in the British Crown Jewels.

events.title: Second Anglo-Burmese War
events.summary: Dalhousie annexes Lower Burma (Pegu) after a short war.
events.detail: A quarrel over the treatment of British merchants at Rangoon gave Dalhousie a reason for war. Rangoon and Pegu were captured and Lower Burma was annexed (1852).
events.yearHook: Burmese wars: 1824, 1852, 1885.

participants.role: Governor-General who annexed Lower Burma.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
causes: Disputes over British merchants at Rangoon.
Dalhousie's policy of expansion.
outcomes: Lower Burma became a British province; Upper Burma followed in 1885.
events.before: Disputes over British traders at Rangoon.
events.after: Dalhousie annexed **Pegu** (lower Burma); the rest of Burma followed in 1885.
events.today: Rangoon (Yangon) grew as a British port city.

events.title: Charter Act of 1853
events.summary: The last Charter Act: civil service jobs opened to open competition, and law-making separated from the executive.
events.detail: The charter was renewed without a time limit — the Company would rule "until Parliament decides otherwise". The Governor-General's council got separate legislative members, the beginning of a legislature in India. Recruitment to the civil service was opened to open competition, and Indians could compete.
course: No 20-year limit this time.
Six legislative members added to the Governor-General's council (the Indian Legislative Council).
Civil service jobs filled by open competition.
outcomes: Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to join the ICS (1863).

pairs.right: Open competition for the civil service

events.yearHook: Charter Acts: 1793, 1813, 1833, 1853 — the last one.

participants.role: Governor-General when the Act was passed.

events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
causes: Demand in Britain to end patronage in appointments.
Need for a separate law-making body in India.
events.before: The Charter Act of 1833 had made the Governor-General of India and ended the Company's trade.
events.after: The **civil service** was opened to competition (1854, **Macaulay Committee**); a separate legislative council began. It was the last Charter Act — 1857 ended the Company.
events.today: **Satyendranath Tagore** (1864) was the first Indian to pass the ICS.

events.title: Wood's Despatch
events.summary: The Court of Directors sends an education despatch, issued by Charles Wood, setting India's education policy (NCERT).
events.detail:
In 1854 the Court of Directors sent an educational despatch to the Governor-General. Issued by Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control, it is known as Wood's Despatch (NCERT). It stressed the practical benefits of European learning — it would create demand for British goods and give the Company trustworthy civil servants (NCERT).

Following it, education departments were set up and steps were taken to set up universities (NCERT).
causes: The Company wanted educated Indians for administration and markets for British goods (NCERT).
course: Education departments set up in every province (NCERT).
Universities planned on the London model.
Grants-in-aid for private schools; teaching in local languages at the school level.
outcomes: Universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were founded in 1857 (NCERT).
facts: Wood's Despatch was issued in 1854 by Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control (NCERT).
Often called the "Magna Carta of English education in India".
Wood's Dispatch 1854 is called the Magna Carta of English education in India.

alsoOn.text: Universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras are founded (NCERT).

events.yearHook: Railway 1853, telegraph and Wood's Despatch 1854 — Dalhousie's "modern" years.

participants.role: President of the Board of Control who issued the Despatch.
Governor-General who received it.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 6
events.before: Macaulay (1835) had promoted English, but there was no full system from schools to university.
events.after: Universities at **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** (1857); grants-in-aid to private schools; vernacular primary schools; women's education. It is called the "**Magna Carta of English education in India**". **Hunter Commission** (1882) and **Raleigh Commission** (1902) followed.
events.today: The three 1857 universities still exist; Madras University counts its start as 5 September 1857.

events.title: Santhal rebellion
events.summary: The Santhals of the Damin-i-Koh rise (1855–56) against zamindars, moneylenders and the colonial state (NCERT).
events.detail:
The British settled the Santhals in the foothills of Rajmahal; by 1832 a large area was demarcated as the Damin-i-Koh, the land of the Santhals (NCERT). But the state levied heavy taxes on the land they cleared, moneylenders (dikus) charged high interest and seized land, and zamindars claimed control over the Damin (NCERT).

By the 1850s the Santhals rose to create an ideal world where they would rule (NCERT). The rising, led by Sidhu and Kanhu, was crushed; villages were burned (NCERT).
causes: Heavy taxes on land the Santhals had cleared (NCERT).
Moneylenders (dikus) charging high interest and taking land (NCERT).
Zamindars asserting control over the Damin (NCERT).
course: 30 June 1855: thousands of Santhals gather at Bhognadih and declare a rising.
They attack moneylenders, zamindars and police posts.
Troops crush the rising; villages are burned and suspects arrested (NCERT).
losses: Santhals: thousands killed; villages burned (NCERT).
outcomes: After the revolt the Santhal Pargana was created — 5,500 square miles carved out of Bhagalpur and Birbhum, with special laws (NCERT).
facts: Santhal rebellion: 1855–56 (NCERT).
Damin-i-Koh was demarcated as Santhal land by 1832 (NCERT).
NCERT names Sidhu Manjhi as the leader.

alsoOn.text: A large area in the Rajmahal foothills is demarcated as the Damin-i-Koh, the land of the Santhals (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1855–56: two years before 1857.

participants.role: Leader of the rebellion (NCERT).
Governor-General when it broke out.

events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes III, Ch. 10 "Colonialism and the Countryside"; NCERT Class 8 Ch. 4
events.before: Santhals cleared the **Damin-i-Koh** (Rajmahal hills) but fell into debt to moneylenders and zamindars.
events.after: Led by **Sidhu and Kanhu**, about 60,000 Santhals rose; the British crushed them and made the **Santhal Parganas** a separate district (1855).
events.today: **Hul Diwas** (30 June) marks the start of the revolt; Jharkhand was formed in 2000.

events.title: Annexation of Awadh
events.summary: Dalhousie takes over Awadh, saying it was misgoverned; Nawab Wajid Ali Shah is deposed (NCERT).
events.detail:
In 1801 a subsidiary alliance had been imposed on Awadh; in 1856 it was taken over. Dalhousie declared that the territory was being misgoverned and British rule was needed (NCERT). The British said they were "obliged by duty" to take over Awadh (NCERT).

Wajid Ali Shah was deposed and sent to Calcutta. Taluqdars lost their estates and sepoys from Awadh felt their homeland had been insulted — Awadh became a centre of the revolt in 1857.
causes: Dalhousie said Awadh was misgoverned (NCERT).
Awadh was rich and lay at the heart of north India.
losses: Awadh: its king; taluqdars lost lands; many courtiers, soldiers and artisans lost their livelihood.
outcomes: The takeover of Awadh in 1856 was expected to complete a process of annexation (NCERT Class 12).
Awadh became a storm centre of the 1857 revolt (NCERT).
facts: Awadh was taken over in 1856 (NCERT).
Grounds: misgovernment — not the Doctrine of Lapse (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Dalhousie's last act (1856) — the revolt came the next year.

participants.role: Governor-General who annexed Awadh.
Deposed and exiled to Calcutta.
His reports on misrule as Resident were used to justify the annexation.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 5 "When People Revolt"; NCERT Class 12 Themes III, Ch. 11 "Rebels and the Raj"
events.before: Wajid Ali Shah was accused of misrule; Awadh had already given half its land (1801).
events.after: Dalhousie annexed it (not by lapse but "misgovernment"). Its soldiers in the Bengal army and its taluqdars lost status — one of the causes of **1857**; **Begum Hazrat Mahal** led the revolt in Lucknow.
events.today: Wajid Ali Shah was sent to Matiaburj, Kolkata, and helped make Kolkata biryani (with potato) famous.

events.title: Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act
events.summary: A law permits Hindu widows to remarry, after a campaign by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (NCERT).
events.detail: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar used the ancient texts to suggest that widows could remarry. His suggestion was adopted by British officials, and a law was passed in 1856 permitting widow remarriage (NCERT). Those opposed to it set up a counter-campaign; few widows remarried at first.
outcomes: Later reformers such as Veeresalingam in Andhra (1881) organised widow remarriages.
facts: A law was passed in 1856 permitting widow remarriage (NCERT).

Other reformers: Derozio and the Young Bengal movement (Hindu College, 1820s–30s); Bethune School for girls (Calcutta, 1849); Gopal Baba Walangkar (Dalit reformer, wrote Vital-Vidhvansak, 1888); the Rakhmabai case 1884 led to the Age of Consent Act (1891); Bankim Chandra's novel Anandmath (1882) gave "Vande Mataram".

The Caste Disabilities Removal Act / Lex Loci Act (1850, Dalhousie) let Hindu converts to Christianity inherit ancestral property; widow remarriage was legalised separately in 1856 (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

alsoOn.text: Kandukuri Veeresalingam performs the first widow remarriage in Andhra (Rajahmundry).

events.yearHook: Sati banned 1829 → widow remarriage 1856.

participants.role: Led the campaign and quoted the ancient texts in support.
Governor-General when the Act was passed.
Carried the cause to Andhra; first remarriage at Rajahmundry (1881).

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 7
causes: The suffering of child widows, who could not remarry (NCERT).
Vidyasagar showed from the ancient texts that widows could remarry (NCERT).
events.before: **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar** used the shastras to argue for widow remarriage and sent a petition with thousands of signatures.
events.after: Lord **Dalhousie** drafted it; **Canning** passed it (July 1856). Few remarriages took place at first; in Andhra **Veeresalingam** arranged the first in 1881.
events.today: Vidyasagar also wrote the Bengali primer "Barnaparichay", still used.

events.title: General Service Enlistment Act
events.summary: Every new sepoy must agree to serve overseas if required (NCERT).
events.detail: Since the Barrackpore refusal of 1824, the issue of crossing the sea had not died down. In 1856 the Company passed a new law: every new person who took up employment in the Company's army had to agree to serve overseas if required (NCERT). Sepoys saw it as a threat to their caste.
outcomes: Added to sepoy anger before 1857 (NCERT).
facts: General Service Enlistment Act: 1856, under Lord Canning.

alsoOn.text: Dalhousie announces that after Bahadur Shah Zafar's death his family will be moved out of the Red Fort (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1856: Awadh annexed, widows allowed to remarry, sepoys made to serve overseas — all in one year.

participants.role: Governor-General who passed the Act.

events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 5 "When People Revolt"
causes: Sepoys kept refusing to go overseas since 1824 (NCERT).
The Company needed troops for Burma and beyond.
events.before: Sepoys of the Bengal army, many high-caste men from Awadh, had served only in India.
events.after: The Act made new recruits agree to serve overseas; with the greased cartridge rumour it fed the anger of **1857**.
events.today: A classic "cause of 1857" in exams: military grievances (GSEA, cartridge, lower pay, no promotion).

events.title: Hyderabad in 1857: Turrebaz Khan and Shorapur
events.summary: In Hyderabad State the revolt is led by Turrebaz Khan, who attacks the British Residency on 17 July 1857; the Nizam's minister Salar Jung keeps the state loyal, and Raja Venkatappa Nayaka of Shorapur rebels in 1858.
events.detail:
Order of events (APPSC key): Mubariz-ud-Daula, the Nizam's brother, was imprisoned in Golconda fort for a Wahabi plot against the British (1839); in June 1857 the 1st Contingent Cavalry at Aurangabad was suspected, disarmed and arrested; Turrebaz Khan and Maulvi Allauddin attacked the Residency (17 July 1857); and Raja Venkatappa Nayaka of Shorapur rose in February 1858.

Turrebaz Khan was later shot while escaping (1859); the Koti area of Hyderabad has a memorial to him. The Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula and Salar Jung I stayed loyal, and the British rewarded the Nizam.
causes: The 1857 revolt spread south; anger at British control of the Nizam's state.
outcomes: The rising was crushed; the Nizam was rewarded with territory.

alsoOn.text: Mubariz-ud-Daula is imprisoned in Golconda fort for a Wahabi plot against the British.
Raja Venkatappa Nayaka of Shorapur rebels against the British.

events.yearHook: 1839 → June 1857 → 17 July 1857 → 1858 (APPSC chronology).

participants.role: Kept Hyderabad loyal.

events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT); APPSC Group-1 2023 key
facts: Andhra was not greatly affected by 1857 — it had no local leaders, and Nizam Afzal-ud-Dowla was pro-British (both true, but the second does not explain the first) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
events.before: Hyderabad had given **Berar** (1853) to pay for the British-officered Hyderabad Contingent; the minister **Salar Jung** was pro-British.
events.after: Turrebaz Khan escaped, was caught and killed (1859). The Nizam got back some land and the title "Faithful Ally".
events.today: A road at Koti, near the old Residency (now the Women's College), is named after Turrebaz Khan.

events.title: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy rises against the Company
events.summary: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy, a poligar family heir of Kurnool district whose allowance had been stopped by the Company, raises a revolt (1846), attacks the treasury at Koilkuntla and fights in the Nallamala hills. He is caught and hanged at Koilkuntla on 22 February 1847.
events.detail:
Background: after the **Ceded Districts** came to the Company (1800), **Thomas Munro** removed the **poligars** (local military chiefs of Rayalaseema) and gave some of them small pensions. Narasimha Reddy's pension was cut, and the new ryotwari taxes hurt peasants.

He gathered thousands of followers, killed officials at Koilkuntla (July 1846) and fought for months. His head was hung on the Koilkuntla fort gate for years as a warning.

Other Andhra resistance under the Company: the **Vizianagaram** raja (Padmanabham, 1794), the **poligars** of Rayalaseema (1800s), and in 1857 **Turrebaz Khan** at Hyderabad.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III ch.5 and 8; Spectrum, A Brief History of Modern India; Bipan Chandra; APPSC topic notes
events.yearHook: 1846: 11 years before 1857; 46 years after the Ceded Districts (1800).
events.before: The Company took Rayalaseema in **1800** and crushed the poligars, who had kept armed men since Vijayanagara days.
events.after: Rayalaseema stayed quiet in **1857**; in Hyderabad **Turrebaz Khan** attacked the Residency (17 July 1857).
events.today: The 2019 Telugu film "Sye Raa Narasimha Reddy" tells his story; Kurnool district remembers him at his village, Uyyalawada.
events.mnemonic: Andhra before 1857 "V-P-U": Vizianagaram raja at Padmanabham (1794), Poligars (1800s), Uyyalawada (1846).
